newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN rights envoys denied prison access in Nigeria.
newsitem.headline: UN rights envoys denied prison access in Nigeria.

text.p: Two U.N. human rights investigators are unlikely to go to Nigeria after the government sent an "unsatisfactory" reply to their request for free access to detention centres, a U.N. spokeswoman said on Tuesday.

Param Cumaraswamy, U.N. special rapporteur on the independence of judges and lawyers, and Bacre Waly Ndiaye, U.N. rapporteur on extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions, were to look into the fate of 19 jailed Ogoni leaders. Linked to the executed author Ken Saro-Wiwa, they face the death penalty.

The mission, invited by the government, had been due to visit Nigeria from February 23 to March 5 in time to report back to the U.N. Human Rights Commission, which opens its annual session on March 10.

The investigators, who also asked to see Moshood Abiola, the presidential claimant who has been jailed on charges of treason since June 1994, expected full access to detainees and dissidents. This was under the normal terms of reference for such fact-finding missions, according to U.N. officials.
An official from the U.N. Human Rights Center has been negotiating in Abuja with Nigerian authorities regarding access.
But a letter received late on Monday at the U.N. Human Rights Center, signed by H.O. Sulaiman, protocol officer at Nigeria's Foreign Ministry, did not appear to grant free access.

"This answer does not appear satisfactory to the two special rapporteurs. It was not satisfactory vis-a-vis the need for access to people in detention," U.N. spokeswoman Therese Gastaut told a news briefing in Geneva.
"At this stage the mission appears unlikely," she added.
Cumaraswamy, a Malaysian lawyer, and Ndiaye, a Senegalese lawyer, are in their respective countries and will decide on Tuesday whether to go to Nigeria, according to the spokeswoman.

Nigeria drew worldwide outrage in November 1995 when it hanged Saro-Wiwa and eight Ogoni minority rights activists after their conviction in the 1994 murder of four pro-government tribal chiefs. Their trial was judged unfair by international judicial experts, but the defendants had no right to appeal.

The mission was to include stops in Lagos, Kano and Kaduna in the north, and Port Harcourt, in the same state as oil-rich Ogoniland, where the 19 Ogoni leaders have been charged with the same four deaths.
